::: {.why}
A risk model that is never tested is a number generator, and the two tests that matter check different failures, one of which almost every model fails.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Run an unconditional coverage test on your VaR exceedances and report the p-value.
- Run an independence test on the same exceedances and say what a rejection tells you about the volatility model behind it.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Implement both tests: the unconditional coverage likelihood ratio on the exceedance count, and the independence test on whether an exceedance predicts the next one. Run them on your three VaR estimators. The historical simulation version usually passes the first and fails the second.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Diagnose the failure: exceedance clustering means the model is not tracking conditional volatility, which is exactly what filtered historical simulation was built to fix. Confirm that the filtered version passes the independence test where the plain historical one does not.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Add the two tests to qlib/risk.py so that any risk model you build later is checkable with one call.
:::
:::

## The running strategy

::: {.project}
qlib/risk.py can now test a risk model rather than only produce one, with coverage and independence tests that any later model has to pass before its numbers are used for sizing.
:::
